title: Map & Plan Labeling
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 2 — Question Type
description: In this question type, you listen to a description of a place (a campus, town, building, park, etc.) and label locations on a map or plan. The speaker gives directions using prepositions, movement verbs, and landmarks.
format: You see a map or plan with some locations already labeled
Several locations are numbered but unnamed
You listen to a monologue (usually a tour guide or orientation speaker)
Three sub-types: (1) Choose the correct letter — identify where places are on a map, (2) Choose the correct label from a word list (more words than gaps), (3) Write up to three words to label places
tips: Read all the labels and look at the map BEFORE the audio plays
Identify the starting point — the speaker usually says 'You are here' or 'Start at the entrance'
Follow the speaker's route — don't jump ahead on the map
Listen for direction words: left, right, straight, past, opposite
Watch out for distractors — the speaker may mention a place then correct themselves
The questions follow the order of the audio — if you miss one, move on
Maps can show streets, building layouts (indoor), or parks/camps — not just roads. Predict what kind of vocabulary you'll hear based on the map type
During preparation time, study the map and try to predict the direction language you'll hear for each gap

title: Form Completion — Furniture Ordering
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 1 — Question Type
description: In Form Completion tasks, you listen to a conversation (usually a phone call or face-to-face enquiry) and fill in missing information on a form or table. You must write no more than the specified number of words and/or a number. This is one of the most common question types in Section 1.
format: You see a form, table, or note with some information already filled in
Several gaps are numbered — you write the missing information
The word limit is stated clearly (e.g., 'NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER')
Answers may be names, numbers, dates, addresses, or short phrases
The questions follow the order of the audio
tips: Read the form BEFORE the audio starts — predict what type of answer each gap needs (a name? a number? a place?)
Pay close attention to SPELLING — names of people, streets, and companies must be spelled correctly
Listen for NUMBERS carefully — phone numbers, prices, and dates are common gap-fillers
Watch the word limit — if it says 'no more than 3 words', an answer of 4 words is WRONG even if the content is correct
Hyphenated words count as ONE word; numbers written as digits do not count as words
Listen for CORRECTIONS — the speaker may say one thing then change it: 'Oh wait, actually it's...'
Table completion follows the same rules — read column headers to know what type of information goes in each cell
Write exactly what you hear — do not change the grammatical form of the words

title: Sentence Completion — Marathon Tips
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 2 — Question Type
description: In Sentence Completion tasks, you listen to a monologue (usually a talk or announcement) and complete sentences with missing words. You must write no more than the specified number of words. The sentences follow the same order as the audio.
format: You see incomplete sentences with gaps for missing words
The word limit is stated clearly (e.g., 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS')
The sentences paraphrase what the speaker says — the exact words in the audio may differ from the sentence
Answers are usually nouns, adjectives, or short phrases from the audio
The questions follow the order of the audio
tips: Read all the sentences BEFORE the audio starts — predict what type of word is missing (noun? adjective? verb?)
The sentences paraphrase the audio — listen for MEANING, not exact word matches
Watch the word limit carefully — 'no more than TWO words' means 1 or 2 words only
Listen for SIGNAL WORDS that tell you the answer is coming: 'firstly', 'the most important thing is', 'make sure you'
If you miss an answer, move on immediately — the next question is coming soon
Write the EXACT words you hear from the audio — don't change the form (e.g., don't change plural to singular)
Check your spelling and grammar after the audio finishes — use the 30-second check time
Numbers and dates count as one word — '10 am' is two words, but '10am' could be written as one

title: Following Directions — Town Map
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 2 — Map Labeling (Streets & Houses)
description: In this exercise, you listen to someone giving directions around a town and label streets and locations on a map. The speaker describes a route using landmarks, road names, and features like traffic lights, roundabouts, and crossroads. There are two separate audio tracks with different routes on the same map.
format: You see a town map with some locations already labeled and lettered points A–K
You listen to two separate sets of directions (two audio tracks)
For each set, you match street names or house locations to the correct letter on the map
There are more lettered options than questions — some letters are distractors
tips: Study the map BEFORE the audio — identify all labeled features (streets, landmarks, traffic lights, roundabout)
Find the starting point — both routes begin from Tanya's house (marked with X)
Follow the route step by step — trace the path with your finger on the map
Listen for turning words: 'turn right', 'turn left', 'sharp right', 'straight on'
Watch for distractors — the speaker may mention an alternative route then say 'but usually I drive down...'
In the second audio, listen for 'forget the first route' — this changes the direction completely
Pay attention to 'on your left' vs 'on your right' — this tells you which side of the road a place is
The questions follow the audio order — if you miss one, move on to the next

title: Identify Distractors
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 2 — Multiple Choice
description: In Section 2 of the Listening test, you hear a recording spoken by one speaker on a topic of general interest. Multiple-choice questions give you three options (A, B or C) and you must choose the correct one. Distractors are words and phrases in the recording that are incorrect answers to a question — they sound relevant but do not actually answer what is being asked. Learning to identify distractors helps you choose the correct answer.
format: Section 2 features one speaker (or mainly one speaker) on a general interest topic
The recording is played in two parts, with questions on each part
Multiple-choice questions have three options: A, B or C — only one is correct
Two types: (1) a question followed by three options, (2) an unfinished statement followed by three possible endings
The questions follow the order of the recording
Distractors are mentioned in the audio but do not answer the question correctly
The correct answer is often paraphrased — the exact words from the question may not appear in the audio
tips: Read all questions and options BEFORE the audio plays — underline key words in each question
Think about what TYPE of information each question asks for (a place? a time? a reason?)
Think of synonyms and paraphrases for the key words — the audio will use different words
Be aware of distractors — don't choose an option just because you hear those exact words in the recording
Listen for SIGNAL phrases that introduce the correct answer: 'they have finally decided to...', 'but actually...', 'the real reason is...'
Listen for phrases that introduce distractors: 'There was talk of... but...', 'you might think... however...'
If you hear all three options mentioned, focus on the CONTEXT — which one actually answers the question?
The questions follow the order of the audio — if you miss one, move on to the next question immediately

title: Flow-chart Completion
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 3 — Question Type
description: In flow-chart completion tasks, you listen to a recording and fill in missing words in a flow-chart that shows a process or sequence of steps. The answers come in the same order as the recording. This task tests your ability to follow a logical sequence while listening.
format: You see a flow-chart with boxes connected by arrows showing a process or sequence
Some boxes have gaps (missing words) that you need to fill in
The word limit is stated clearly (e.g., 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS')
The answers follow the order of the recording
You may be given a word list to choose from, or you may need to use words from the recording
The flow-chart may contain technical or scientific language — don't panic, focus on the words you DO understand
tips: Read the ENTIRE flow-chart before the audio plays — understand the overall process first
For each gap, predict the TYPE of word needed (noun, verb, adjective) based on the grammar around it
Read the words BEFORE and AFTER each gap — they give strong clues about the missing word
Listen for signposting words that signal a new step: 'first', 'next', 'then', 'finally', 'the last thing'
The recording may use synonyms or paraphrases for words in the flow-chart — don't expect exact matches
If the flow-chart uses technical language, the speaker will often explain the terms — listen for the explanation
Check your spelling and word count — writing too many words means the answer is marked WRONG
If you miss an answer, move on — the next step in the flow-chart will be coming soon

title: Cambridge 16 Listening Test 1 — Part 1
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Section 1 — Note Completion
description: In this Section 1 task, you listen to a conversation about Children's Engineering Workshops and complete the notes with ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER. The notes are organized into sections — read ahead before the audio starts to predict what kind of information is missing.
format: You see notes with gaps numbered 1–10
The notes are organized by topic (age groups, activities, logistics)
You write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer
Answers come in the same order as the questions
Some information is already filled in to help you follow along
tips: Read ALL the notes before the audio starts — predict what type of word is missing (noun? number? day?)
The words before and after each gap are your signposts — listen for them in the audio
Answers are usually everyday words — don't overthink spelling
If you hear a number, check whether the gap expects a number or a word (e.g., 'five' vs '5')
Section 1 is the easiest — use it to build confidence and get into the rhythm
If you miss an answer, move on immediately — the next question is coming

title: End-of-Course Test — Part 1
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Sections 1 & 2 — Cambridge IELTS 19 Test 1
description: Part 1 of the end-of-course listening test covers Sections 1 and 2 with 20 questions. Section 1 is a note completion task about Hinchingbrooke Country Park. Section 2 has multiple choice questions about the Stanthorpe Twinning Association and a map labeling task for Farley House.
format: Section 1 (Q1-10): Note completion — Hinchingbrooke Country Park
Section 2 (Q11-15): Multiple choice — Stanthorpe Twinning Association
Section 2 (Q16-20): Map labeling — Farley House
tips: You hear each section ONCE only — there is no replay in the real test
For note completion: predict the word type (noun, number, adjective) from the context
For multiple choice: read all options before listening — eliminate wrong answers as you hear the audio
For map labeling: study the map and identify the starting point before listening
Section 1 is the easiest — use it to build confidence
Write answers as you listen — don't wait until the end

title: End-of-Course Test — Part 2
subtitle: IELTS Listening — Sections 3 & 4 — Cambridge IELTS 19 Test 2
description: Part 2 of the end-of-course listening test covers Sections 3 and 4 with 20 questions. Section 3 is a discussion about recycling footwear with multiple choice and matching questions. Section 4 is a lecture about tardigrades with note completion.
format: Section 3 (Q21-24): Multiple choice — Recycling Footwear
Section 3 (Q25-28): Matching — Reasons for rejecting footwear
Section 3 (Q29-30): Multiple choice — Recycling Footwear
Section 4 (Q31-40): Note completion — Tardigrades
tips: Sections 3 and 4 are harder — stay focused and don't panic if you miss one
For matching: read ALL the options (A-F) before listening so you recognize them
Section 4 is a monologue about an academic topic — the vocabulary is more advanced
For note completion with 'ONE WORD ONLY': never write two words, even if tempting
The questions follow the order of the audio — if you miss one, move on
Use any preparation time to read ahead
